newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour slams government on food safety.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour slams government on food safety.

text.p: Labour leader Tony Blair said on Friday the government should be ashamed of its record on food safety and promised that if elected he would set up a food standards agency to restore public confidence.

Speaking at the Labour Party's Scottish conference, Blair warned his party to take nothing for granted in the run up to the election, even though it enjoys a commanding lead in the opinion polls over the ruling Conservative party.
"There is only one opinion poll that matters and that is the one on election day. I am and remain the eternal warrior against complacency," Blair said.

"Even if we win, there will be no victory dances. For then, the hard work in serving our country begins in earnest. And we shall approach that task with the same dedication and high-mindedness that we showed in creating new Labour," Blair added.

He said the government's handling of food scares in the past year showed an administration that was in decay and "utterly incapable of providing leadership or competence." Agriculture minister Douglas Hogg, already under fire for his handling of the mad cow crisis, denied to parliament on Thursday that he had suppressed a damaging report on unhealthy conditions in abattoirs that could have spread disease to meat supplies. The issue is particularly sensitive in Scotland, where 20 people died recently from E.coli food poisoning.

Professor Hugh Pennington, a scientist appointed by the government to look into the outbreak, said it was "potty," that he had not been told about the report into abattoir conditions, which could have helped him in his investigation.
Blair recalled that Major had told him in parliament that there was no need to publish the report. The prime minister went on to accuse the Labour leader of not understanding how government works.
A furious Blair countered on Friday: "If I was in charge of an organisation, let alone a government, which behaved like this government, I would be ashamed."
He said the food standards agency would be a powerful, open and transparent consumers' champion that would act as a single point of contact for government, consumers and the food industry.
"It should cover all areas from production to transport to storage. All the way from plough to plate," Blair said.
Blair re-committed a Labour government to legislating for a Scottish parliament in its first year of office.
He brushed aside the concerns of left-wing activists about Labour's proposed tight spending limits by insisting that Labour would need to clean up the financial mess left by the Conservatives.
Scotland is one of the few remaining strongholds of the old-style socialist ideas that Blair has ruthlessly rooted out since he became Labour leader in 1994 and set about wooing middle class voters.
Blair offered no comfort to left wing activists hoping that Labour would go back to its radical roots if and when it wins the election.
"We run for office as New Labour. We govern as New Labour. No going back to the past. Not old left or new right but a new centre and centre-left agenda for Britain.
